name: Tamil
confidence_why: Arden 1910 gives the emphasis to a long-vowel syllable and otherwise to the first syllable, Rhenius 1846 puts it on long or closed syllables and denies any accent in all-short words, Andronov 1989 calls Modern Tamil stress weak, free and movable with many short non-initial syllables stressed, and Keane 2003 and 2007 find only weak, non-contrastive prominence on the initial syllable while stating that the literature has no consensus on whether Tamil has word stress at all or where it falls.

But when all the vowels in a word are short, or all long, the emphasis is always thrown upon the first syllable. In many English words the emphasis is thrown upon the second syllable, as in the words support, refresh, corrupt. Great care must be taken not to do this in Tamil; but the emphasis must always be thrown upon the first syllable; as மரம் [maram] a tree, அனுப்பு [aṉuppu] send (thou). sweep_summary: Two Glottolog title hits for Tamil, neither read and neither likely about word stress. Pittman 1971 ('Tense vs. lax word-base prosodies.. Tamil retroflexion vs. Hindi aspiration') is a Firthian/SIL feature-domain paper in Vol. I of the 1968 Madras Tamil Studies proceedings; only Vol. 2 is open (archive.org tdl.22993), and its preface, contents and printed pp. 249-253 were read from saved page scan to confirm the paper is not there; Google Books gives the opening sentence only (no page view). Thananjayarajasingham 1974 ('Adjectival system in Jaffna Tamil: a prosodic analysis', Indian Linguistics 35: 31-43) is Firthian prosodic analysis of adjective morphology in the Sri Lankan dialect, print only, no open copy anywhere found. Both marked unclear/low priority; no new first-hand stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title, so the catalog's Arden 1910 deciding source (already flagged at-risk by the prior check on Andronov 1989 and Keane 2003/2007) stands unchanged by these two titles. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books API, HathiTrust, fatcat and scholar.archive.org metadata, Crossref, and the Google Books GData feed. and.

new_statements.quote: 13. Every long vowel, or every compound syllable, by which I mean a syllable composed of two consonants and a vowel, has naturally a particular emphasis or accent. Thus in காது, kāthŭ, the ear, the syllable கா has the stress; in சொல்லுகிறேன், sŏllŭgirēn, I say, the syllables சொல் and றேன் have the stress. Besides this natural emphasis, Tamil syllables have no accent. In words, consisting of two or more short syllables, every such syllable is pronounced alike. Samscrit words of three syllables are often written in Tamil with four syllables; e. g. அவச்யம், is written அவசியம்; in this case the emphasis of the Samscrit is retained, thus: pronounce ăvăsĭyăm.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tamil has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement among the listed works. It is compatible with the on-disk Andronov 1989 line 'In words with a long vowel it is generally stressed' (sec. 10, p. 29) but goes further in denying any accent in all-light words. Describes 1840s Tamil as taught by the Tirunelveli mission; no dialect named.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence is a property of heavy syllables: every syllable with a long vowel, and every closed ('compound', CVC) syllable, carries stress, and more than one heavy syllable in a word can be stressed (both சொல் and றேன் in sŏllŭgirēn). Apart from this, Tamil has no accent: a word made only of short syllables has all its syllables pronounced alike, i.e. no word stress at all. (Rhenius's own transcriptions were checked against the page scan, p. 33.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the example sŏllŭgirēn gives stress to two heavy syllables in one word without ranking them.
new_statements.exceptions: Sanskrit loanwords written with an extra syllable in Tamil keep the Sanskrit emphasis (ăvăsĭyăm). The preceding para. 12 (pp. 17-18) is about vowel quantity ('measures'), not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Beschi 1822 describes Shen-Tamil (centamil), the literary high dialect, not spoken Tamil; Rhenius 1846 is a general grammar of the Tamil of the 1840s (Tirunelveli mission), no dialect named; Asher 1989 (not opened) treats standard modern Tamil.

readall_conflicts: Among the five listed works only Rhenius 1846 speaks, and it gives a weight-based rule (long-vowel and closed syllables carry stress; all-short words have no accent). Andronov 1989 (sec. 10, pp. 28-29) calls Modern Tamil stress 'weak, movable, free' with its place 'not fixed', gives stressed short syllables (["veyil], [tA"mIzh] vs ["tAmIzh]), while also saying long-vowel syllables are 'generally stressed', that a secondary stress appears in words with several heavy syllables, and that Classical Tamil stress was 'fixed on the initial syllable'; Keane 2003 (ICPhS) states there are no stress-based lexical contrasts, that earlier impressionistic work reached no consensus, and that word-initial syllables resist vowel reduction. So the sources held by the project range over weight-sensitive (Rhenius), free/lexical (Andronov) and initial-prominence-without-lexical-stress (Keane); the listed works themselves contain no internal conflict because only one of them was both open and informative.

audit.recode_to: conflict ('descriptions disagree'), leaning hedged weak initial prominence if the catalog privileges instrumental over impressionistic sources: impressionistic descriptions split between a vowel-length/quantity-conditioned movable stress (Arden 1910 para. 29; Andronov 1989 sec. 10 'weak, movable, free.. place not fixed.. long vowel generally stressed', with speaker variation) and fixed initial stress (Keane 2003: 'most descriptions favour either fixed initial stress or a quantity-sensitive dynamic system'), while every instrumental study held (Keane 2003, 2006 abstract, 2007) finds weak, non-lexical, weight-blind word-INITIAL prominence (Keane 2007: L turning-point inside the initial syllable in 465 of 467 phrase-medial tokens in a design that systematically varied syllable quantity, incl. light-heavy words). Do not keep weight class CVV as the classification of record unless Christdas 1988 or Keane 2006 full text states a length condition that survives the instrumental evidence.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: Arden 1910 paras 29 and 81 are verbatim on the held archive.org page scan (pp. 17-18, 30) and djvu scanned; Keane 2004, Keane 2006 abstract and Schiffman 1999 passages are in the copies we hold at the stated lines. (2) The deciding source is a 1910 missionary teaching grammar; the weight condition (CVV heavy) and the initial default both come only from it. sources.note: The letters section treats only vowel quantity (short/long, the mātra 'measure of time', abbreviated vowels, lengthening for metre); nothing on stress, accent or prominence. The scanned's only 'stress' hit is 'Little stress is laid upon the observance of this rule' in the poetics part, and 'deep tone' there refers to the close of a stanza; 'accent' does not occur. Describes Shen-Tamil, the literary high dialect, not the spoken language.
